newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Nordbanken proposes five bln crown buy back.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Nordbanken proposes five bln crown buy back.

text.p: Sweden's state-controlled Nordbanken on Wednesday proposed a five billion crown ($741 million) share buy back that could reduce the government's holding to 58 percent from 65.5 percent.

The bank's managing director Hans Dalborg said the buy-back, at a price three percent below the market price, would increase earnings per share and should have a positive impact on the company's share price.

"The increased profit per share should be positive for the market share price which will improve our chance to take an active part in the continuing restructure of Sweden's financial sector," Dalborg said in a statment.
Trading in Nordbanken was suspended on Wednesday morning before the Swedish bourse opened, pending the announcement.
Its shares closed on Tuesday at 135.5 crowns. Trading resumed at 1115 GMT on Wednesday and by 1300 GMT the share was up 12.5 crowns at 148.
Nordbanken said the buy back offer would be open from September 23 to October 11.
"The Swedish state has already pledged to participate in the buy back process with all its share holding which in fact guarantees the entire proposed buy back," the bank said.
Nordbanken was taken over wholly by the state in 1992 after being hit the hardest by a loan-loss crisis that swept through the Swedish banking system.
In 1995 the state sold off 34.5 percent capital in the bank and has frequently expressed its intention to dispose of the rest of its stake.
The bank said the buy back would reduce the number of shares by 15-18 percent to 176.5 to 182.7 million from the current 215 million shares.
The buy-back would be priced at about three percent below a range of 130-155 crowns a share.
"At this price the buy back can be more beneficial for the state than if it was carried out on the open market," Nordbanken said.
Bank chairman Jacob Palmstierna said the bank intended to use remaining capital for further expand.

"It is the board and management's view that the remaining capital is easily enough for possible future expansion, especially considering the bank's continuing profitability," Palmstierna said in a statement.
Nordbanken posted an 18 percent jump in profits after credit losses in the first half of 1996 to 3.8 billion crowns.
Credit losses fell to 260 million crowns compared to 661 million crowns in the same period a year earlier.
The bank said its shareholders' equity currently totalled 19.7 billion crowns, built up over the past few years, which was too high.

"A well balanced reduction of our shareholders' equity will improve the possibilities to maintain profitablity and at the same time maintain development possibilities," the bank said in its statement.
